title: Acquired inheritance is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans
dek: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — change only the RNA in the brain and you alter behavior three generations later.
why: 35 minutes walks through the conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers; the mammalian part repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a takeaway you can apply.
who: People working in reproductive health, IVF diagnostics, or epigenetics; and biology readers who want to know whether Lamarck was completely wrong.
skip: The three sponsor segments can be skipped.

points.h: The genome is the whole book; each cell takes one page
points.body: Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room has an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out just one page — that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually codes for proteins is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome codes for messenger RNA, while a huge amount of transcribed RNA does other things, many of which remain unknown. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and the remaining question is whether life experience can rewrite those instructions.

points.h: Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
points.body: Why, by default, can't what you learn be passed down? Rechavi attributes this to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can pass information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates various chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — about 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for erasing is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being limited to the few pieces a particular room has made.

points.h: It was opposed and desired, not entirely for data reasons
points.body: This barrier theory made acquired inheritance long unfashionable. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory — the barrier is there; the other is the atmosphere created by the controversy itself. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, yet also wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: what you do doesn't affect the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it's promising’ — he only says RNA is a new clue, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in mammalian research.

points.h: Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
points.body: Why trust nematodes? Rechavi's list of conditions is very specific: a C. elegans always has 959 cells, 302 of which are neurons, and since the 1980s there has been a complete connectome, like a subway map showing who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can directly watch neurons fire, and you can use optogenetics to switch genes on and off; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, grown in petri dishes on bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

points.h: Offspring can't make small RNAs, yet still resist viruses
points.body: The experimental design is clean enough to judge by color: use a fluorescent virus, so if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, and if it's eliminated it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by the virus and eliminate it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in the offspring — these offspring cannot make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happened: all offspring stayed black, and the resistance could be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents had been infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses using RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

points.h: The brain and inheritance don't use the same language
points.body: The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just be removing a particular odor receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it down; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been convincingly proven, because no one has explained how information travels from the brain to the germ cells. His own approach bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of natural small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them for up to three generations, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically transports RNA.

Why can nematodes do it while mammals are doubted? Rechavi's mechanism is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can continuously amplify these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known similar amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how can a tiny amount of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are only a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and then step by step it steers development off course, with problems like metabolism following. This is the idea of the developmental origins of health and disease. He also describes the role of RNA in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, time will tell’.

points.h: RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
points.body: Applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples planning to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but currently no one looks at RNA; if the mechanisms become clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, with some RNAs possibly linked to disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed like DNA — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. The next step is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; during IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of what you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it's figured out, he imagines telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, which would change your RNA profile.

quotes.text: This is like the IKEA book that you have in every cell in your body, the instructions to make everything that you need in your house, the chairs, the kitchen, the pictures. But in every room, you want something else.

The man who first thought about this barrier is called Weismann, August Weismann. … Separation of the soma from the germline, only the germline transmitting information to the next generation. And this is also called the second law of biology.

So to preserve this, we erase all these modifications and start anew. And this is in mammals and in humans, this is largely true. Most of the modifications in the sperm and in the egg are removed, so about 90% of them.

In the worm, we now have very obvious and clear-cut proof that there is inheritance of acquired traits. So much so that I don't think that anyone pretty much in the epigenetic field argues against it.
We demonstrated this very clearly using a fluorescent virus. If the virus replicates successfully, the worm just turns green, and if the virus is destroyed, the worm stays black.
What we did in C. elegans is we showed that the brain can communicate with the next generations using small RNAs, and that this can change behavior.

For example, there are experiments in rodents where they show that overfeeding the rodents creates problems for the next generations, for the children. However, if you let the rodent exercise, then it corrects the aberrant inheritance.
The beauty is that this, unlike DNA, it's plastic. So with DNA, this is your DNA, perhaps we can choose another embryo.
